analysis.one_liner: Provides grants of up to $20,000 to first-generation first-time homebuyers for downpayments and closing costs.
analysis.headline: The bill sat in the House Financial Services Committee for the entire 18-month Congress and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created a $100 billion federal grant program, run through HUD and state housing agencies, to help first-time homebuyers whose parents never owned a home. Qualified buyers could get up to $20,000 — or more in high-cost areas — toward a downpayment, closing costs, or a lower mortgage rate, with priority shaped toward closing the racial homeownership gap. It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee on the day it was introduced and no further action was ever taken.
analysis.who_benefits: First-time homebuyers whose parents or guardians never owned a home, including adults who grew up in foster or institutional care, as long as their household income is under 120% of the area median (140% in high-cost areas). The bill also authorizes larger amounts for buyers who are socially and economically disadvantaged, and funds mandatory homebuyer counseling. Because eligible loans must meet Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, FHA, VA, Rural Housing, or qualified-mortgage standards, mainstream mortgage lenders would gain a large new stream of well-qualified, subsidized borrowers.

how_it_helps.text: Provides each qualified first-generation, first-time homebuyer a one-time grant of up to the greater of $20,000 or 10% of the purchase price, with the cap raisable for socially and economically disadvantaged buyers and for homes in high-cost areas, to cover downpayment, closing costs, or interest-rate buydowns.

Directs 75% of funds to states by formula and 25% competitively to eligible entities — minority depository institutions, community development financial institutions, mission-driven nonprofits, and local governments — with the formula weighted toward states with more potential qualified buyers and higher home prices.

Targets buyers whose parents never owned a home and adults who have been in foster or institutional care, with the stated purpose of addressing multigenerational inequities and narrowing the racial homeownership gap; grantees can be stripped of funds if distributions predictably bypass racial and ethnic groups that have historically faced obstacles to homeownership.

Protects buyers who move or sell early: repayment is only proportional to years occupied up to five, is waived entirely after five years of occupancy, and is waived when a hardship or a low-profit sale means the buyer cannot cover it.

Requires approved homeownership counseling before purchase, with at least 5% of appropriated funds reserved for counseling, and requires referral and re-qualification counseling for any buyer denied an eligible mortgage.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through an authorization of $100 billion in appropriations that would remain available until spent. Because a downpayment subsidy adds purchasing power for a fixed supply of homes, part of the benefit could also be passed through to home sellers as higher prices, and the lenders originating the eligible mortgages would earn the interest on the larger loans.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers, via a $100 billion authorization

drawbacks.text: The bill authorizes $100 billion in new spending with no funding source attached — it would still require Congress to appropriate the money — and reaching households up to 120% of area median income (140% in high-cost areas) extends the subsidy well into the middle class, raising the cost.

Eligibility for 'first-generation' status rests entirely on the borrower's self-attestation, the bill bars creditors from any liability for lending to someone who in fact did not qualify if they relied in good faith on that attestation, and no documentation beyond the attestation may be required — a design that invites misuse.

A downpayment subsidy aimed at a limited housing supply can push purchase prices up, meaning part of the $20,000 grant would reach sellers and lenders rather than making homes genuinely more affordable; the bill contains no supply-side construction provisions to offset this.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real and targeted: a $20,000 grant is often the difference between renting and owning for a family that can afford a monthly mortgage payment but not the downpayment, and the five-year occupancy forgiveness and mandatory counseling are sensible guardrails. But the design carries three honest costs: a $100 billion authorization with no revenue source, income eligibility that reaches middle-income households, and a pure demand-side subsidy in a market with a housing shortage, which risks inflating prices rather than expanding ownership. The self-attestation rule with a blanket liability shield for lenders is the weakest part — it trades program integrity for administrative speed.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced, the Republican-controlled committee never took it up, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Representative Maxine Waters of California, the ranking Democrat on the House Financial Services Committee, introduced the bill on June 21, 2023 with three original cosponsors: Representatives Al Green of Texas, Sylvia Garcia of Texas, and Ayanna Pressley of Massachusetts.
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services, where Waters was the senior minority member and Republicans held the majority.

Over the next 18 months, 57 House Democrats cosponsored the bill; the action history records no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action, and no Senate companion movement before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No constituency gained anything concrete: the program simply never existed, and no money was ever appropriated. The parties that benefit from the status quo are federal taxpayers, who avoided a $100 billion authorization, and incumbent homeowners and mortgage lenders, who did not face a new wave of subsidized competition for homes — while the first-generation buyers the bill was written for got nothing.

for.name: Maxine Waters
for.role: Ranking Member, House Financial Services Committee
for.what_they_did: Sponsored and introduced the bill; as the committee's senior minority member she had no ability to schedule action on it.

for.name: Al Green, Sylvia Garcia, and Ayanna Pressley
for.what_they_did: Joined Waters in introducing the bill on its first day.

for.name: 57 of 216 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no House Republican did.

against.name: Patrick McHenry
against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee to which the bill was referred; the committee took no action on it — no hearing or markup is recorded — for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: House Republican majority
against.what_they_did: Controlled the committee calendar and House floor; not one of the 224 House Republicans cosponsored the bill and it was never brought to a vote.

sides.party_line_note: All 57 cosponsors were House Democrats; not one of the chamber's 224 Republicans signed on, and with Republicans chairing the Financial Services Committee the bill never reached a vote in either chamber.

industries.note: The bill only funds loans meeting Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, FHA, VA, Rural Housing, or qualified-mortgage standards, so originators would gain tens of thousands of subsidized, counseled borrowers — larger loans financed partly by taxpayers. The liability shield for lenders who rely on borrower self-attestation would shift verification risk away from the industry.

industries.industry: Home sellers and the real estate industry
industries.note: Adding up to $20,000 of purchasing power per eligible buyer in a market with limited supply tends to raise sale prices and commissions, meaning part of the subsidy would be captured by sellers rather than buyers.

industries.industry: Housing counseling agencies and nonprofit housing intermediaries
industries.note: The bill reserves at least 5% of all funds for pre-purchase counseling, and community development financial institutions, minority depository institutions, and mission-driven nonprofits would be eligible to receive and administer grants directly.
Each state's housing finance agency would be the default administrator of 75% of the funds by formula, with an allowable share for administrative costs and a 1% capacity-building set-aside.
